source_refs.note: Exercise 12.2, Question 3: continuity at x = 2 and x = -2 (book p.233). Answer key PDF 310 labels the two answers (i), (ii) and wrongly says discontinuous at x = 2.

blocks.prompt: 3 If \[f(x) = \begin{cases} 3x, & x \le -2 \\ x^2 - 1, & -2 < x < 2 \\ 3, & x \ge 2 \end{cases}\]discuss continuity at \(x = 2\) and \(x = -2\).
blocks.explanation:
A continuity question at two points of a three-piece function.
At each point where the formula changes we test the three conditions separately.
Plan: (a) at \(x = 2\): \(f(2)\), LHL, RHL; (b) at \(x = -2\): the same.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = 3x\) for \(x \le -2\), \(x^2 - 1\) for \(-2 < x < 2\), \(3\) for \(x \ge 2\).
To find: whether \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 2\) and at \(x = -2\).
Method: \(f\) is continuous at \(x = c\) when three conditions hold: (i) \(f(c)\) is defined, (ii) \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\) exists (LHL = RHL), (iii) \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)\). If any one fails, \(f\) is discontinuous at \(c\).

(a) At \(x = 2\): find \(f(2)\)
\[f(2) = 3\]
Why: \(x \ge 2\) includes 2, so the constant piece 3 gives \(f(2)\).

(a) Left hand limit at 2
\[\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 2^-} (x^2 - 1)\]
\[= 4 - 1 = 3\]
Why: Just left of 2 we are in \(-2 < x < 2\), the middle piece.

(a) Right hand limit at 2
\[\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 2^+} 3 = 3\]
Why: Right of 2 the function is the constant 3; the limit of a constant is the constant.

(a) Conclusion at \(x = 2\)
\[\text{LHL} = \text{RHL} = 3 = f(2)\]
Why: All three conditions hold, so \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 2\). The parabola reaches height 3 exactly where the flat line starts.

(b) At \(x = -2\): find \(f(-2)\)
\[f(-2) = 3(-2) = -6\]
Why: \(x \le -2\) includes \(-2\), so the first piece \(3x\) is used.

(b) Left hand limit at \(-2\)
\[\lim_{x \to -2^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to -2^-} 3x\]
\[= -6\]
Why: Left of \(-2\) (like \(-2.01\)) the first piece is used.

(b) Right hand limit at \(-2\)
\[\lim_{x \to -2^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to -2^+} (x^2 - 1)\]
\[= (-2)^2 - 1 = 3\]
Why: Right of \(-2\) (like \(-1.99\)) we are in the middle piece. Note \((-2)^2 = +4\).

(b) Conclusion at \(x = -2\)
\[\text{LHL} = -6\]
\[\text{RHL} = 3\]
\[-6 \ne 3\]
Why: The one-sided limits differ, so \(\lim_{x \to -2} f(x)\) does not exist; condition (ii) fails and \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x = -2\) (the graph jumps from \(-6\) up to 3).

Check
\[f(1.99) = 3.9601 - 1 = 2.9601\]
\[f(-2.01) = -6.03,\ f(-1.99) = 2.9601\]
Why: Near 2 both sides are close to 3; near \(-2\) the two sides are far apart, confirming the jump.
blocks.final_answer: \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 2\) and discontinuous at \(x = -2\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints "(i) \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x = 2\)". This is wrong: at \(x = 2\) the left hand limit is \(2^2 - 1 = 3\), the right hand limit is 3 and \(f(2) = 3\), so \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 2\). The key's "(ii) \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x = -2\)" is correct.
